opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest change is that you lose the safety net, and that turns out to be both scary and very clarifying.

At a big company, a lot of the hard questions are already answered for you. There's a brand, a customer base, infrastructure, a recruiting machine, legal, finance. Your job is to do one piece of the puzzle really well. When I was working on large-scale AI systems, the challenge was mostly technical: how do we make this framework faster, how do we serve this many users, how do we make the platform reliable. Those are deep problems, but the surrounding context is fixed.

When you start a company, nothing is fixed. You have to ask, "Why would anyone care about this?" every single day. Product, pricing, hiring, fundraising, even what to put on the website: all of it is now your problem. As an engineer, my instinct is to fix things by writing better code. But in a startup, the bottleneck is often not the code. It's whether you understand the customer well enough, or whether you picked the right problem in the first place.

The second big shift is speed. At a large company, a decision might take weeks because many teams need to align, and that's reasonable when the stakes are huge. At a startup, if we don't decide by Friday, we've lost a week of runway. So you learn to make decisions with incomplete information, to be okay being wrong, and to correct quickly. That was a mindset adjustment for me.

Third, the relationship with technology changes. In a big company, you can sometimes build technology for its own sake because it might pay off long-term. In a startup, technology must serve the business directly. That's actually been healthy for me. It forces you to think about what really matters to users, not just what's elegant.

And personally, the sense of ownership is very different. When something goes wrong, there's no one else to escalate to. But when something works, like when a customer tells you your product saved them weeks of work, that feeling is much more direct. That's a big part of why I made the jump. In AI especially, the landscape is moving so fast that I felt the best way to learn and contribute was to be right at the front, building with a small team, close to the users.

r001.rationale: The response says big companies can build technology for long-term payoff, but does not explain that expected continued existence enables this work.

r002.rationale: It mentions startup runway and the cost of delay, but does not clearly state that the short planning horizon makes survival a primary concern.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest change is that nobody hands you a problem anymore. At a place like Facebook or Alibaba, the infrastructure is there, the users are there, the data is there, and your job is to be very good at one slice of it. I spent years thinking about how to make a framework run faster, and that was a well-defined, well-supported problem.

When you start a company, the first thing you discover is that the hard part isn't the technology. The hard part is figuring out what people will actually pay for, and then being honest with yourself when the answer is "not this." In a big company you can be right about the technology and still be fine. In a startup you can be right about the technology and still die, because you picked the wrong customer or the wrong timing.

The second change is scale of decision-making. At a big company, a wrong decision costs you a quarter. At a startup it can cost you the company, but you also get to make ten decisions a day instead of one a month. That speed is addictive. You go from optimizing a system to optimizing a whole organism, including yourself.

And the last thing, which I didn't expect, is how much it changes your relationship with open source and the community. When I was doing Caffe or PyTorch, the community was the point. Now the community is still the point, but you also have to think about how the company survives so that you can keep giving back. Those two things don't always pull in the same direction, and learning to balance them is maybe the most interesting part of the job.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts decision costs at large companies with startups, but does not explain that large companies’ expected continued existence enables longer-term work.

r002.rationale: It says a startup can die from a wrong decision and must consider how the company survives, but does not connect a short planning horizon to survival being a primary concern.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that you can’t take the surrounding infrastructure for granted anymore. In a big company, you have a team, a budget, and an established way of reaching customers. You’re usually trying to solve a problem within that system. As an entrepreneur, figuring out which problem is worth solving—and whether someone actually needs your solution—is part of your job.

That also changes how you think about technology. As engineers, we naturally want to build something technically elegant. But when you’re starting a company, you have to ask: Does this help the customer enough that they’ll use it and pay for it? Sometimes a relatively simple solution creates much more value than a sophisticated one.

So I see it as a shift in responsibility. You have more freedom to choose a direction, but you also have to make sure that direction makes sense. The feedback is more direct, and you have to be willing to change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts big-company infrastructure with entrepreneurial responsibility, but does not say that large companies’ expected continued existence enables longer-term work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a small company’s short planning horizon or survival as a primary concern.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the biggest change is that you have to create the structure yourself. At a big company, you usually have a team, resources, and a fairly clear scope. As an entrepreneur, you have to decide what problem matters, who you’re solving it for, and how to bring the right people together to solve it.

That also changes how you think about technology. Something can be technically very interesting, but you still have to ask: Does somebody need this enough to use it, and eventually pay for it? You need that feedback much earlier.

I still see a lot of continuity, though. You’re working with people to build something useful. The difference is that in a startup, the distance between a decision and its consequences is much shorter. That’s challenging, but it’s also what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts big-company resources and scope with entrepreneurship, but does not say that large companies’ continued existence enables longer-term work.

r002.rationale: It says startup decisions have quicker consequences and require earlier feedback, but does not explain that a short planning horizon makes survival a primary concern.
